title: Load Balancing
subtitle: Distribute requests across healthy instances using workload-aware routing
objectives: Explain what a load balancer buys you, and why it's indirection rather than speed
Choose a distribution algorithm based on whether requests and servers are uniform
Describe how health checks fail — including evicting healthy machines under load
Reason about the balancer as its own single point of failure, L4 vs L7, and why sticky sessions are a smell

exercises.title: A load balancer maps one client endpoint to a pool of servers
exercises.body: Clients connect to the load balancer's stable address. For each connection or request, it selects an eligible backend, forwards the traffic, and returns the backend's response. Backend addresses and pool membership remain internal, so servers can be added, removed, or replaced without changing the client endpoint.
exercises.note: Draining removes a backend from new selections while allowing its in-flight requests to finish, which prevents routine deploys from terminating active work.

exercises.prompt: A failed server still receives one-third of requests. Make the load balancer stop routing to it after failed health checks.
exercises.beforeStatus: SUCCESS RATE · 67% · one of three routes is dead
exercises.afterStatus: SUCCESS RATE · 100% · traffic splits across two healthy servers
exercises.result: Health-aware routing stopped sending traffic into failure
exercises.why: Health checks let the load balancer remove an unresponsive server from rotation. Detection is not instantaneous, and an overloaded but healthy server can fail aggressive checks, so intervals and thresholds affect both recovery time and false eviction.

exercises.prompt: Assemble the system for this case: A failed server still receives one-third of requests. Make the load balancer stop routing to it after failed health checks. Place Load balancer, Server A, Server C. Then connect the components in the direction that requests, data, or events move.
exercises.why: The completed diagram contains these directed flows: Clients → Load balancer; Load balancer → Server A; Load balancer → Server C. That topology is the evidence for the answer: Health checks let the load balancer remove an unresponsive server from rotation. Detection is not instantaneous, and an overloaded but healthy server can fail aggressive checks, so intervals and thresholds affect both recovery time and false eviction.

exercises.prompt: You now run 3 identical app servers. Your users only know one address. What has to exist?
choices: Something in front that receives every request and picks a server to hand it to
The servers must merge into one machine
Each user must be given a different address
exercises.why: A load balancer presents one service address, accepts incoming requests, and routes each request to a member of the server pool. Clients remain independent of individual server addresses, so pool membership can change without changing the public endpoint.

exercises.prompt: A ______ balancer presents one address to clients and distributes requests across many servers.
exercises.why: A load balancer exposes one address while selecting among multiple backend servers. That indirection hides the pool's size and membership from clients.

exercises.prompt: Match each thing a load balancer gives you.

pairs.right: Clients don't know or care how many servers exist
A server can finish its work before leaving

exercises.why: The stable address decouples clients from backend membership, distribution shares requests across the pool, health checks stop routing to failed servers, and draining lets a departing server finish in-flight work. Together these functions allow routine pool changes without interrupting requests.

exercises.prompt: Beyond spreading load, what does a load balancer let you do that's arguably more valuable day to day?
choices: Take a server out of rotation — to deploy, patch, or replace it — without downtime
exercises.why: Removing a server from rotation stops new assignments to it while other servers continue serving traffic. The isolated server can then be deployed, patched, or replaced without taking the service endpoint offline, provided the remaining pool has enough capacity.

exercises.prompt: Your load balancer sends requests to 3 servers. One is much slower than the others — but it's not down. What does the LB do about it?
choices: Nothing automatically — 'slow' isn't 'dead', and a basic health check only asks whether it responds
It sends the request to all three
exercises.why: A basic health check classifies a server by whether it responds before a configured timeout. A slow server can still pass that binary test and continue receiving work, so detecting degraded latency requires a check or routing policy that measures more than reachability.

exercises.prompt: What does adding a load balancer NOT do?
choices: Give you one address for many servers
Let you remove a server without downtime
Stop sending traffic to a dead server
exercises.why: A load balancer chooses a backend; it does not reduce the computation that backend performs. One request still incurs the backend's processing time and may add a routing hop, while aggregate throughput can rise because requests are distributed across servers.

exercises.title: A balancing algorithm selects a backend from the eligible pool
exercises.body: *Round robin* increments through the server list and distributes request counts evenly when pool membership is stable. It does not measure request cost or current server work. Least-connections routing instead selects the server with the fewest active connections.
exercises.note: Round robin can overload a server when requests have highly variable duration, because equal request counts can produce unequal concurrent work.

exercises.prompt: Round-robin sends equal requests to two servers, but Server A's requests take 20ms and Server B's take 400ms. Route new work using active connections.
choices: Keep round-robin and retry slow requests
Pin each client permanently to one server
choiceFeedback: Retries add more work to the already busy server and equal rotation still ignores the 5-versus-80 signal.
Active connection count reflects the unequal request durations and lets the busy server drain.
Permanent affinity can preserve the imbalance and makes server removal harder.
exercises.beforeStatus: IN-FLIGHT · Server A 5 · Server B 80 · still receives equal new traffic
exercises.afterStatus: IN-FLIGHT · new traffic favors Server A until pressure converges
exercises.result: Routing responded to unequal request duration
exercises.why: Least-connections routing uses current in-flight work as a load signal, which helps when request durations differ. It can still misjudge work when one connection is far more expensive than another.

exercises.prompt: Complete the system for this case: Round-robin sends equal requests to two servers, but Server A's requests take 20ms and Server B's take 400ms. Route new work using active connections. Place Server A, Server B. Then connect the components in the direction that requests, data, or events move.
exercises.why: The completed diagram contains these directed flows: Least connections → Server A; Least connections → Server B. That topology is the evidence for the answer: Least-connections routing uses current in-flight work as a load signal, which helps when request durations differ. It can still misjudge work when one connection is far more expensive than another.

exercises.prompt: The simplest algorithm: send request 1 to server A, request 2 to B, request 3 to C, then back to A. What's it called, and what does it quietly assume?
choices: Least connections — it assumes servers are identical
Round robin — it assumes every request costs about the same
Hashing — it assumes users are evenly spread
exercises.why: Round robin assigns requests in a fixed rotation and therefore equalizes request counts. Equal counts approximate equal load only when requests consume similar time and resources; long-running requests can accumulate unevenly because the algorithm does not observe current work.

exercises.prompt: Match each algorithm to what it does.

pairs.right: Send to the server with the fewest active connections
Bigger servers get a larger share
The same key always lands on the same server

exercises.why: Round robin rotates assignments, least connections uses active connection count as a load proxy, weighting gives higher-capacity servers more traffic, and key hashing provides repeatable placement. A server with fewer connections can still be busier when its requests cost more, so connection count is not a direct measurement of CPU or latency.

exercises.prompt: Your requests vary wildly: most take 5ms, some take 30 seconds. Which algorithm handles that better?
choices: Least connections — it notices a server is still busy with a slow request and routes around it
exercises.why: A 30-second request keeps its connection open, increasing that server's observed connection count. Least connections routes new work toward servers with fewer open connections, so it responds to uneven request duration when connection count is a useful proxy for load.

exercises.prompt: Your fleet has a mix: some machines have 8 cores, some have 32. Which approach fits?
choices: Weighted — give the bigger machines a proportionally larger share
exercises.why: A 32-core server can accept a larger traffic share than an otherwise comparable 8-core server, so weighted balancing represents their unequal capacity. Weights must be measured and maintained because hardware capacity, request mix, and downstream limits can make CPU count an imperfect proxy.

exercises.prompt: Why might you hash a user's id to pick their server, instead of balancing by load?
choices: Because you want that user to land on the same server repeatedly — for a warm local cache, say
It spreads load more evenly than round robin
exercises.why: Hashing the user identifier deterministically selects a server, so repeated requests can reuse that server's local cache. This placement constraint can create uneven load, and membership changes remap users unless the hashing scheme limits movement.

exercises.prompt: Which algorithm is 'best'?
choices: None: it depends on whether requests cost the same, whether servers are the same, and whether placement matters
exercises.why: Algorithm choice depends on request-cost variance, server-capacity variance, and whether repeatable placement is required. Round robin suits similar requests on similar servers; least connections reacts to ongoing work; weighting models unequal capacity; and hashing preserves affinity.

lessons.title: Retrying through a balancer still creates new work

exercises.title: A balancer redistributes retries; it does not make them free
exercises.body: Retrying another server can escape one failed instance, but every retry consumes fleet capacity. Passive health removes bad targets, while retry budgets and backoff prevent clients from converting partial failure into whole-fleet overload.
exercises.note: Use an end-to-end budget so nested services cannot each multiply attempts.

exercises.prompt: Clients send 10,000 req/s. Half would retry once after a failed attempt; healthy capacity is 12,000 attempts/sec. Drag the *smallest* retry share prevented by budgets and passive health that avoids overload.
exercises.why: Unbounded single retries create 15,000 attempts/sec. Preventing 60% of retry attempts leaves 12,000. Removing unhealthy targets reduces failed first attempts, while budgets stop remaining failures from multiplying load.

lessons.title: Move load before a server queues

exercises.title: Balancing changes each server's arrival rate
exercises.body: Two servers can each handle 7,000 requests/sec. Sending all 12,000 requests/sec to Server A overloads it while Server B sits idle. The balancer must move enough requests that every server's arrival rate stays at or below capacity.
exercises.note: Equal request counts work here because the requests have equal cost. Real balancers may need latency or active-work signals.

exercises.prompt: Traffic is 12,000 req/s. Server A handles at most 7,000 req/s. Drag the *smallest* share to Server B that keeps Server A alive.
exercises.why: At 41%, Server A still receives 7,080 req/s and overloads. At 42%, it receives 6,960 req/s, below its 7,000 req/s capacity. The remaining 5,040 req/s goes to Server B.

exercises.title: Active health checks control which backends receive traffic
exercises.body: The load balancer sends a probe such as `GET /health` to each backend at a configured interval. A timeout, status check, and failure threshold classify the backend as unhealthy and remove it from selection. A success threshold admits a recovering backend again.
exercises.note: A shallow probe can admit a server whose dependencies are broken; a deep probe can evict all backends that depend on one failed shared service.

exercises.prompt: Show the minimum components and flows that implement this mechanism: Active health checks control which backends receive traffic
exercises.why: The load balancer sends a probe such as `GET /health` to each backend at a configured interval. A timeout, status check, and failure threshold classify the backend as unhealthy and remove it from selection. A success threshold admits a recovering backend again. A shallow probe can admit a server whose dependencies are broken; a deep probe can evict all backends that depend on one failed shared service.

exercises.prompt: How does the load balancer know a server has died?
choices: The server tells it before crashing
It checks — periodically asking each server whether it's alive, and removing those that fail
It doesn't; an engineer has to remove it
exercises.why: An active health check periodically probes an endpoint such as `/health`. After the configured failure threshold, the balancer removes an unresponsive server from rotation; periodic success checks can later return it to the pool.

exercises.prompt: Your `/health` endpoint just returns `200 OK` unconditionally. What's the problem?
choices: Nothing — it proves the server is up
It proves the web server can answer, not that the app can do its job — a server with a dead database connection passes happily
exercises.why: An unconditional `200 OK` proves that the process and route can respond, while a real request may still fail because a required dependency is unavailable. Health checks should cover dependencies necessary for serving, while a shared dependency must be handled carefully because its failure could mark every server unhealthy simultaneously.

exercises.prompt: Under heavy load your servers get slow, so health checks start timing out. The LB removes those servers. What happens next?
choices: The remaining servers get the same traffic across fewer machines, so they get slower and fail checks too — the fleet unravels one machine at a time
exercises.why: Timed-out checks remove servers while incoming demand remains unchanged. The same load is then divided across fewer servers, increasing their latency until they also miss the timeout; this positive feedback produces a cascading failure. Eviction thresholds or a minimum healthy-pool floor can limit the cascade.

exercises.prompt: Which are real risks of health check configuration? Select all.
choices: Too shallow: broken servers keep serving traffic
Too deep: one shared dependency failing removes the entire fleet at once
Too aggressive: brief slowness under load evicts healthy machines
exercises.why: A shallow check can admit a server that cannot serve real requests. A check coupled to shared dependencies can evict the whole fleet during one dependency failure, and short timeouts or low failure thresholds can evict healthy servers during transient slowness. The configuration balances detection speed against false eviction.

exercises.prompt: You're deploying. You want to stop sending new requests to a server but let it finish the ones it's already handling. What's that called?
exercises.why: Draining removes a server from new request selection while allowing its existing requests to complete before shutdown. This prevents deploys or maintenance from terminating in-flight work and producing avoidable gateway errors such as `502 Bad Gateway`.

exercises.prompt: A server that failed its health check recovers and rejoins the pool. What's the risk?
choices: It can be handed a rush of traffic before it's warmed up — cold caches, empty connection pools — and immediately fall over again
exercises.why: A recovered server may have cold caches and empty connection pools, so its initial requests cost more than requests on warm peers. Giving it a full traffic share can overload it and trigger another failure; slow start ramps its share while those resources warm.

lessons.title: A balancer cannot route to capacity that does not exist

exercises.title: Fleet capacity is healthy instances multiplied by measured per-instance capacity
exercises.body: A load balancer chooses destinations; it does not create processing capacity. Six servers at 3,000 requests/sec each provide 18,000 requests/sec only while requests have the measured cost and all six instances remain healthy.
exercises.note: Operating exactly at the arithmetic limit leaves no room for bursts or one failed server.

exercises.prompt: Traffic is 18,000 req/s. Each interchangeable server sustains 3,000 req/s. Choose the *fewest* healthy servers the load balancer needs.
exercises.why: Five servers provide 15,000 req/s and overload. Six provide exactly 18,000. A production fleet keeps additional failure and burst headroom rather than operating at this mathematical minimum.

exercises.title: Load-balancer availability requires redundant balancers and traffic failover
exercises.body: Deployments run multiple load balancer instances and provide a way for clients to reach a surviving one. DNS can publish several addresses, a floating virtual IP can move to a standby, and anycast can route the same address to another site. The failover mechanism sits outside the failed balancer.
exercises.note: Failure detection and address convergence determine outage duration; stale DNS caches or routing state can keep sending traffic to a failed instance.

exercises.prompt: Remove the load-balancer single point of failure. Build an entry path that can route clients through either balancer to the app pool.
exercises.why: The anycast address is an entry mechanism outside either balancer and can route clients to a surviving load-balancer instance; both balancers reach the same app pool. If the design has only one balancer, its failure still removes the sole request path even though every app server is healthy; stale routing convergence can also extend the outage after failover begins.

exercises.prompt: Match each load balancer type to what it can do.

pairs.right: Routes by IP and port, without reading the request
Reads the HTTP request — can route by path or header

exercises.why: A Layer 4 balancer routes transport connections using network addresses and ports, with relatively little per-connection processing. A Layer 7 balancer parses application data such as HTTP paths, hosts, headers, or cookies, enabling content-aware routing at additional processing cost.

exercises.prompt: Sessions live in each server's local memory, so users break when they land on a different machine. Someone suggests sticky sessions — pinning each user to one server. Is that a fix?
choices: It's a workaround: it hides the symptom by making your servers non-interchangeable, which is the property you were relying on
Yes, and it also improves load distribution
exercises.why: Sticky sessions route a user back to the server holding that user's local session, so ordinary requests can succeed. The session remains tied to one failure domain, and affinity can skew load or complicate draining; a shared session store restores server interchangeability.

exercises.prompt: Your app keeps sessions in local server memory and it's hurting. Slide toward your approach.
exercises.rightLabel: Move sessions to a shared store (real fix, more work)
exercises.why: Moving sessions to a shared store lets any healthy server serve a user, which supports balanced routing, autoscaling, and draining. Sticky sessions require less immediate change but preserve dependence on one server, so the answer range favors shared storage while allowing affinity as a temporary migration measure.

exercises.prompt: A load balancer distributes traffic across servers. So can it protect you from a traffic spike bigger than your whole fleet can handle?
choices: No — it spreads load; it doesn't reduce it. Distributing 10× traffic across 3 servers just overloads all 3 evenly
Yes, it queues the extra requests forever
Yes, if you use least connections
exercises.why: A load balancer redistributes incoming work but does not reduce its total cost. If demand is ten times the fleet's capacity, even distribution overloads every server; protection requires additional capacity or admission control such as rate limiting and early rejection with `429 Too Many Requests`.

exercises.prompt: Users report intermittent errors during every deploy. You use round robin, no draining, and health checks every 30 seconds. What's the most likely cause?
choices: Round robin is the wrong algorithm
Servers are being killed mid-request, and for up to 30 seconds the LB keeps sending traffic to machines that are already gone
exercises.why: Without draining, stopping a server terminates its in-flight requests. Until the next health check detects the shutdown, the balancer may also assign new requests to that server; with a 30-second interval, this routing gap can last nearly 30 seconds.

exercises.prompt: What's the honest summary of load balancing?
choices: It makes your system fast and highly available automatically
It gives you one address and disposable machines — and hands you new decisions: which algorithm, how to check health, and where the single point of failure moved to
It's only needed above a million users
It removes the need for health checks
exercises.why: A load balancer turns a changing server pool into one service endpoint and enables distribution, health-based routing, and draining. Its design still requires an algorithm suited to the workload, health-check thresholds that avoid false eviction, and redundancy for the balancer tier itself.

exercises.prompt: Two rendering workers receive equal job counts, but one gets ten-minute videos and the other ten-second clips. Which policy uses the better load signal?
choices: Round robin by job count only
Least active work or measured load
exercises.why: Equal counts do not mean equal remaining work when job cost varies. Active-work, queue-depth, or latency signals better represent the actual imbalance.
